setupSteps: Warm up first. 1 to 3 minutes of ankle circles, gentle hip hinges and a few easy mini-squats (see Bodyweight squat, Home 1) or one round of Tadasana breathing.
Floor. Flat, non-slip mat or bare floor with grip; avoid slippery socks on tiles.

Stand in Tadasana. Feet together (big toes touching, heels slightly apart) for the classic form, or hip-width (about two fists apart, est.) for steadier balance and easier knees. Beginners should start hip-width.
Weight. Spread the weight evenly over the whole foot, then shift it slightly back toward the heels.

Support (optional). Wall: stand with the back to the wall and walk the feet about 2 feet (60 cm) out, so the pelvis, ribs and shoulders can touch as you bend; farther from the wall makes it deeper (teaching sources, snippets). Chair: stand in front of a sturdy chair with the seat behind you, hips hovering just above or lightly touching the seat. Block: hold between the thighs for alignment.
Arms. Beginners start with hands together at the chest or hands on the hips; raise the arms overhead only if the shoulders are comfortable.
Clothing. Stretchy pants; no tight jeans; fitted top so the camera sees the shoulders and hips.
Camera. Phone on a stool or shelf at about hip height, 2 to 2.5 m to the side, so the whole body from head to feet is in frame (see sections 11 and 12).

steps.title: Stand tall
steps.action: stand in Tadasana, feet hip-width, arms by the sides.
steps.feel: the whole sole of each foot pressing down, spine long.

steps.title: Set the weight
steps.action: feel the weight settle into the heels without lifting the toes.
steps.feel: the arches lifting a little, the toes spread and relaxed.

steps.title: Soften the knees
steps.action: bend the knees a small amount first (a shallow chair).
steps.feel: the front of the thighs switching on lightly.

steps.title: Send the hips back and down
steps.action: sit the hips back and down as if lowering onto a low chair, keeping the spine long and the chest lifted.
steps.feel: the buttocks and thighs working; the weight staying in the heels.

steps.title: Draw the lower belly in
steps.action: gently draw the lower belly in and up to support the lower back; keep the ribs soft, not flaring.
steps.feel: a light brace around the waist, no big arch in the lower back.

steps.title: Check the knees
steps.action: knees over the second toe, hip-width, not caving in. A block between the thighs can help.

steps.title: Bring the arms up (optional)
steps.action: on an in-breath, reach the arms forward and up beside the ears, palms facing in, or keep hands at the chest.
steps.feel: shoulders away from the ears, ribs not pushed forward.

steps.title: Hold
steps.action: stay with a slow, even nose breath. Beginners about 5 breaths (about 25 seconds, est.); sources range from a few breaths to 30 to 60 seconds.
steps.feel: steady burn in the thighs, no pain in the knees or lower back.
steps.breathing: slow nose breaths, count each out-breath; never hold the breath.

steps.title: Stand up
steps.action: on an in-breath, press through the heels and straighten the legs, arms coming down (or staying up if the shoulders are fine).
steps.feel: thighs and buttocks driving the lift.

steps.title: Rest
steps.action: shake out the legs, stand in Tadasana or fold forward gently with bent knees.

commonMistakes.title: Lifting the heels or tipping onto the toes
commonMistakes.text: Lifting the heels or tipping onto the toes. It loads the front of the knees and ruins balance. Fix: shift the weight back, wiggle the toes, and sit the hips farther back.

commonMistakes.title: Knees caving in
commonMistakes.text: Knees caving in. It stresses the inside of the knee. Fix: knees over the second toe; squeeze a block lightly between the thighs.

commonMistakes.title: Pushing the knees far forward past the toes
commonMistakes.text: Pushing the knees far forward past the toes. Sources disagree on whether this is harmful, but it commonly means the hips are not sent back and the load shifts to the knee joint. Fix: send the hips back, soften the bend, hinge forward from the hips, and keep the heels down.

commonMistakes.title: Over-arching the lower back
commonMistakes.text: Over-arching the lower back. Pushing the tailbone out and the ribs forward compresses the lower back. Fix: draw the lower belly in and up, tailbone slightly down.

commonMistakes.title: Rounding the back or collapsing the chest
commonMistakes.text: Rounding the back or collapsing the chest. It loses the point of the pose. Fix: lift the chest, keep the spine long, and lean forward from the hips only.

commonMistakes.title: Shrugging the shoulders or looking up with the chin lifted
commonMistakes.text: Shrugging the shoulders or looking up with the chin lifted. It strains the neck. Fix: shoulders down, gaze forward.

commonMistakes.title: Holding the breath
commonMistakes.text: Holding the breath. It raises effort and blood pressure. Fix: slow nose breathing for the whole hold; Harvard Health advises coming out of a pose briefly if held longer than about 10 seconds with high blood pressure (snippet).

commonMistakes.title: Going too deep too soon
commonMistakes.text: Going too deep too soon. Knee or thigh pain follows. Fix: shallow depth, use the wall or chair, add depth gradually.

commonMistakes.title: Standing up fast
commonMistakes.text: Standing up fast. Dizziness can follow. Fix: rise slowly on an in-breath.

safetyNotes: Moderate effort, never joint pain. Stop at pain in the knee, back, hip or shoulder.

Knees: keep the weight in the heels, knees over the second toe, and do not collapse inward. Sources advise avoiding or going very shallow with chronic knee pain, arthritis, damaged ligaments or a recent knee, ankle or foot injury (snippets; one gives under two months as a caution). Use a shallow depth or the wall, and ask a doctor or physio.
Lower back: do not over-arch; draw the lower belly in and keep the spine long. Stop if pain spreads or leg tingling or numbness appears.
Shoulders: skip the overhead arms if the shoulders are sore; keep hands at the chest.

Blood pressure and heart: Harvard Health says blood pressure rises during yoga, especially with quick movement or longer holds, and advises moving slowly between poses and briefly coming out of a pose if held longer than about 10 seconds (snippet; chair pose not discussed). Sustained isometric effort and breath-holding are plausible raisers of blood pressure (our inference, not a source statement). Use short holds, never hold the breath, rise slowly.
Dizziness or headache: a few sources list headache or insomnia as cautions for the pose (snippet). Stop, rest and sit down.
Stop immediately if you feel: sharp knee or back pain, numbness or tingling, dizziness, chest pain or breathlessness, a pop or pull.
Spotter: not needed. Gym etiquette: keep the mat and block out of the walkway; do not take the only mat in a crowded stretching area for long.

Hold time: a few breaths, 30 to 60 seconds, or one breath in a dynamic class. We chose about 5 breaths (about 25 s, est.).
Knees past toes: a long-standing cue versus research-based views that allow it. We chose weight in the heels, knees over the second toe, hips back, and no hard rule.
Feet together or hip-width: classical versus modern teaching. We chose hip-width for beginners.
Arms: overhead versus hands at the chest. We chose hands at the chest for beginners.
Low blood pressure: allowed with slow rising versus listed as a caution. We chose "rise slowly".

Not found: official CYP or MDNIY text for Utkatasana (it appeared not to be a CYP posture, but only from summaries); a chair-pose-specific MET; measured joint-angle norms for the held yoga pose; the full text of the Liu et al. 2021 EMG values; clinical sources for osteoporosis, postpartum, thyroid, cholesterol and heart disease for this pose; ACOG wording; a direct comparison with the bodyweight squat. Our thresholds are estimates.
Most pages were seen only as search snippets or summaries; direct page fetches were not possible.
